purpose: Fixed vocabulary injected into Guild pattern-translation prompts. A wrong entry silently corrupts every translation that uses it, so every entry carries a source and a confidence.

confidence_levels.project: Already shipped in js/i18n.js. This is our own decision and translations MUST match it.
confidence_levels.high: Established English term, confirmed by two or more independent English-language sources.
confidence_levels.medium: Established but context-dependent, or confirmed by only one source. Review before relying on it.
confidence_levels.pending: Tier B. No English equivalent exists. Treatment not yet decided by LuthierTN.

entries.source: trimax:Manual of Leather Goods p.98; jlia:924; leatherworker.net:86486; patent:US2539051; arsutoriaschool
entries.gloss_draft: a gusset that runs up one side, across the bottom and up the other, so the front and back panels never meet
entries.note: VERIFIED in the primary source: Manual of Leather Goods p.98 names three types — 'side gussets, continuous gussets and folded gussets' — matching JLIA's 横まち／通しまち／折れまち in name and number. CAVEAT ON MEANING: the manual defines a continuous gusset as joined at the sides, TOP and bottom, whereas Japanese consumer usage of 通しマチ (kawanowa, sot-web, munekawa) is sides and bottom only — which that manual would call a FOLDED gusset. Keep the edge list explicit in the gloss so an English reader trained on the manual is not misled. Alternatives: 'wraparound gusset', 'T-gusset' (leathercrafthaven), 'through gusset' (munekawa's own English site). Arsutoria School independently names this 'side-bottom (Italian: fianco-fondo) — side and bottom panels form a single piece', which is the sides+bottom sense, not the manual's sides+top+bottom.

entries.gloss_draft: a gusset tapering narrower toward the bottom, named for the shape of a bamboo leaf
entries.note: munekawa's English site romanizes this 'Sasago gusset' and glosses it; 'tapered gusset' is clearer for a UI label. sot-web's 'sasara-machi' reading is wrong.

entries.gloss_draft: a boxed gusset that closes the opening as it folds, used on coin compartments so coins cannot spill
entries.note: We already call this a box gusset in our own design notes. Also written 函マチ.

entries.gloss_draft: a bellows gusset folded like an accordion, with the dividers set in the valleys of the folds
entries.note: 風琴 is a reed organ, which works by bellows — and leathercrafthaven defines a bellows gusset as 'the accordion's tailored cousin, shaped so the pleats collapse cleanly', matching how Japanese treats 風琴マチ as the more refined accordion. CAVEAT: this JA-EN pairing is our inference from the two definitions, not a documented equivalence, and 'bellows' does not by itself encode the real distinction (dividers in the valleys for 風琴, on the peaks for 蛇腹). Needs LuthierTN's confirmation as a maker. kawanowa's 'fūgin' reading is wrong; 風琴 is ふうきん.

entries.gloss_draft: an accordion gusset with the dividers set on the peaks of the folds rather than the valleys
entries.note: leathercrafthaven gives 'accordion/concertina' as one type. Dividers sit on the peaks of the folds, versus the valleys for 風琴マチ.

entries.gloss_draft: an accordion gusset whose top edge spreads open in a fan
no side gusset at all: the depth comes from a triangular fold at each bottom corner
a gusset at the top face rather than the sides or bottom
a narrow band joining the body panels to the opening or zip section, rather than a gusset folded out of the body itself
entries.note: Same structure as 捨てマチ — confirmed by LuthierTN (2026-09-18) and by Sakai workS: 「いわゆる'帯マチ'とか'捨てマチ'等と言われる構造」. The professional English term names the CONSTRUCTION, not the part: Arsutoria School defines 'Strip Construction' as 'a small band of leather or fabric acts as a connection between two main parts of the bag'. 'Strip gusset' is our part-name derived from it. Note English has no everyday word for this because a plain English gusset IS a strip; Japanese needs 帯 only because it also has gussets folded out of the body (笹・三角・折れ).

entries.gloss_draft: a gusset whose side and bottom panels are separate pieces, not continuous with the body

entries.source: jlia:924; trimax:Manual of Leather Goods p.98
entries.gloss_draft: a gusset on each side only, leaving the front and back panels joined at the bottom
entries.note: Agrees across both primary sources: JLIA '両側のまちを独立させた横まち'; Manual of Leather Goods p.98 'Side gussets are joined at the sides of the article'.

entries.source: jlia:924; trimax:Manual of Leather Goods p.98; leathercrafthaven
entries.gloss_draft: a gusset split in two down its height, each half joined to the front and back panels so it folds shut
entries.note: Named in both primaries but defined differently: JLIA says the gusset is halved vertically and joined to the left and right of the front and back panels; Manual of Leather Goods p.98 says folded gussets are 'joined at the sides and bottom'. These may not be the same construction — confirm before using. Reading unverified.

entries.gloss_draft: a narrow band joining the body panels to the opening or zip section; set back so it does not read as a gusset from outside
entries.note: RESOLVED 2026-09-18: LuthierTN uses it in the same sense as 帯マチ, matching Sakai workS. See 帯マチ for the full reasoning. Rejected 'welted gusset': an English welt sits PROUD of the seam, while 森革工房 describes this tucking inward (「うまく引っ込むように作るのがポイント」) — opposite directions. The Reddit thread often cited for a 捨てマチ↔welted gusset equivalence could not be verified (blocked to both fetchers).

entries.gloss_draft: gathering the slack at a turned rounded corner into fine, even radial pleats
entries.note: JLIA defines it but leaves its English field EMPTY — even the industry body declined to translate it. English craft sources use 'kikuyose' as a loanword. Japanese alias: キザミ (kizami). Suggest label 'Radial Corner Pleating', with kikuyose in the gloss.

entries.gloss_draft: a brand of polyester sewing thread; always spelt Vinymo
entries.note: A brand name, not a word: it is never translated. Without this entry the translator gave four different spellings in three runs — Vinymo, Vinio, Binimoⓡ and Binimoファイル. With it, Vinymo six times out of six.

entries.gloss_draft: a tannery and its vegetable-tanned leather; always spelt Tochigi Leather
entries.note: A tannery name. Without this entry German left it in Japanese; with it, Tochigi Leather six times out of six.

entries.gloss_draft: a cylinder-arm sewing machine, for sewing tubes, bags and other closed shapes
entries.note: Without this entry the translator invented "wrist stitcher". It is a machine with a narrow cylindrical arm, not anything worn.
